title: Free Enterprise Fund v. Public Company Accounting Oversight Board
lead: An accounting firm challenged its federal overseer before receiving a sanction. The Supreme Court allowed that structural suit and struck down one layer of removal protection, preserving the oversight board and its powers under a more accountable appointment structure.

actors.name: Beckstead and Watts
actors.role: Nevada accounting firm inspected and investigated by the Board.

actors.name: Free Enterprise Fund
actors.role: Organization to which the firm belonged and fellow plaintiff.

actors.name: Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB)
actors.role: Five-member regulator created by the Sarbanes-Oxley Act.

actors.name: Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)
actors.role: Agency appointing and supervising Board members.

actors.name: Justice Breyer
actors.role: Dissenter joined by Stevens, Ginsburg, and Sotomayor.

proceedings: The district court heard the constitutional suit but granted the Government summary judgment; a divided D.C. Circuit affirmed. The Supreme Court affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded, severing Board-member removal restrictions while sustaining the appointment arrangement as modified.
limits: The Court assumed commissioners’ for-cause protection because the parties agreed, although the SEC statute did not expressly provide it. It did not dismantle the Board, authorize direct presidential removal of its members, or decide the reserved civil-service, adjudicator, and military questions. Dissent appendix counts describe 2010 sources.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Congress creates an accounting regulator with two asserted layers of protected tenure
sections.cue: What powers and safeguards did the statute supply?
paragraphs: After major accounting failures, Congress created the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) in the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) appointed five members to staggered five-year terms. Firms auditing public companies had to register, pay fees, follow Board rules, and submit to inspections, investigations, discipline, and serious sanctions. Despite statutory language placing the Board outside the federal government, the parties agreed it was governmental for constitutional purposes and its members were officers exercising significant authority.

The SEC approved or could alter rules and sanctions and exercised budgetary and other supervision. Individual members, however, could be removed only on restrictive good-cause grounds: willful violations, willful abuse, or unreasonable failure to enforce compliance, determined on a record after notice and a hearing opportunity.

The SEC’s own statute did not expressly protect commissioners against removal. The parties agreed that for-cause protection existed, and the Supreme Court decided on that understanding. The second layer was therefore an assumption, not a holding finding express tenure language in the SEC statute.

sections.title: An inspected firm seeks constitutional review before being sanctioned
sections.cue: How did the courts first respond?
paragraphs: The Board inspected Beckstead and Watts, a Nevada accounting firm, criticized its auditing procedures, and opened an investigation without imposing a sanction. The firm and Free Enterprise Fund, an organization of which it was a member, sought declaratory and injunctive relief challenging the Board’s structure and appointments. The United States intervened.

The district court found jurisdiction but entered summary judgment for the Government. A divided D.C. Circuit affirmed, with Judge Kavanaugh dissenting. The Supreme Court addressed access to court before reaching presidential control and appointment authority.

sections.title: The ordinary securities review scheme does not supply meaningful review of this claim
sections.cue: Why did the firm not have to invite a penalty first?
paragraphs: Section 78y provided appellate review of SEC rules and final orders. Under Thunder Basin, the precedent governing implied review-channel exclusivity, the Court considered meaningful review, whether the claim was collateral, and agency expertise.

No sanction existed to appeal, and petitioners did not have to incur one deliberately to challenge the regulator’s constitutionality. An appeal from an unrelated Board rule was not a meaningful means to contest the Board’s existence. The structural questions lay outside the SEC’s technical expertise and were collateral to ordinary agency orders.

Established equitable relief against unconstitutional official action supported both the Appointments Clause and separation-of-powers theories; there was no reason to distinguish them for this purpose. The conclusion permitted this structural suit, without abolishing statutory review or exhaustion requirements for regulatory claims generally.

sections.title: The majority finds the added layer incompatible with presidential accountability
sections.cue: How did it distinguish existing removal precedents?
paragraphs: Chief Justice Roberts wrote for Justices Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, and Alito. Executive power and faithful execution required presidential supervision and electoral accountability for executive officers. The majority relied on the Decision of 1789 and Myers while declining to reconsider Humphrey’s Executor, Perkins, or Morrison, which permitted some single-level tenure protections.

With one protected level, the President or a directly accountable subordinate could determine whether cause existed. Here protected commissioners controlled whether separately protected Board members met especially rigorous removal criteria. The President could assess commissioners’ conduct but ordinarily could not override their reasonable judgment that cause was absent. The extra layer weakened responsibility for the Board’s executive authority and suggested the possibility of still more layers diffusing command.

Efficiency and expertise did not excuse that structural problem. Congress’s control over offices, duties, and salaries made presidential supervision important to constitutional balance. Broader readings of the removal terms were unpersuasive, and supervisory control over functions did not replace control over members. Changing rules, budgets, or jurisdiction was cumbersome and did not give effective control over individual investigations.

sections.title: The Court removes the tenure restriction rather than the regulator
sections.cue: Why did the remaining appointment scheme survive?
paragraphs: The Court severed §§7211(e)(6) and 7217(d)(3), the substantive restrictions on removing Board members. Ordinary appointment power carried removal authority, leaving the SEC able to remove them at will. The statute remained workable, and neither text nor history established that Congress would prefer no Board. The Court declined broader redesign of duties or appointments.

With at-will removal and existing supervision, Board members qualified as inferior officers under Edmond, the precedent emphasizing supervision of such officers. The SEC was a freestanding, self-contained executive component and thus a department for appointment purposes. Commissioners collectively exercised its governing power; the chair did not command colleagues. A multimember body could serve as a department head and validly appoint the Board.

The chair’s agreement with previous appointments did not defeat standing because the Court could not assume identical choices if the chair alone held authority. Commission approval could also satisfy the clause for other appointments initially made by the chair. Those observations did not invalidate those appointments.

sections.title: The majority expressly leaves other institutions and constitutional classifications open
sections.cue: What did its structural rule not decide?
paragraphs: The Board’s substantial executive power and unusual protection mattered. The Court did not determine other employees’ officer status, invalidate civil-service protections, resolve administrative law judges’ status or removal terms, or decide presidential power over military officers.

It also reserved whether the SEC counted as an executive department for the Opinions Clause or Twenty-Fifth Amendment. The appointments holding did not answer every use of department elsewhere in the Constitution.

sections.title: Breyer assesses actual control rather than counting protected layers
sections.cue: Why did the dissent find the existing structure sufficient?
paragraphs: Justice Breyer dissented with Justices Stevens, Ginsburg, and Sotomayor. He agreed Board members were inferior officers but considered text, history, and precedent insufficiently conclusive to justify a mechanical two-layer rule. He favored functional examination of the President’s ability to perform constitutional duties, respecting congressional administrative expertise. Congress had not assigned removal to itself.

Removal was only one instrument of influence. Independent commissioners would not have to obey presidential wishes simply because Board protection vanished. Meanwhile the SEC already controlled rules, investigations, sanctions, budgets, and responsibilities. The change offered little demonstrated practical benefit. Expertise, impartial adjudication, and public confidence justified independence, and Perkins and Humphrey’s Executor together with functional precedents supported the design.

sections.title: The dissent questions the broader consequences and the assumed second layer
paragraphs: Breyer warned of uncertain consequences for civil servants, administrative adjudicators, and military officers and doubted that severability would neatly resolve every later application. His appendices identified forty-eight agencies or offices with statutory protection, an illustrative 573 senior protected appointees, 1,584 administrative law judges, and twenty-seven agencies with other independence features but no express removal protection. These were the dissent’s historical counts and characterizations, with source-date and time-lag cautions, not current totals or majority findings.

Because the SEC statute was silent, Breyer also criticized assuming commissioners’ protection and then using that assumption to invalidate another statute. He would sustain the Board’s protection whether or not commissioners possessed implied tenure safeguards.

sections.title: The Board survives under at-will SEC removal authority
sections.cue: What relief did the Supreme Court permit?
paragraphs: On June 28, 2010, the Supreme Court affirmed the D.C. Circuit in part, reversed in part, and remanded. Petitioners were entitled to declaratory relief ensuring regulation by a constitutionally accountable agency, but not a broad injunction dismantling Board operations.

The 5–4 result preserved the Board and its substantive authority while removing one layer of tenure protection. It neither invalidated Sarbanes-Oxley wholesale nor empowered the President to remove Board members directly. The wider removal precedents and expressly reserved institutional questions remained for other cases.
